video_title: Why OOP Exists: Localize State and Behavior
core_insight: OOP is not about classes, it is about localizing state with its invariants and behavior behind a contract so change is bounded and understandable as the system grows.

scenes.voice: Why does OOP exist at all? It is not for syntax.
scenes.visual: Title card with code sprawl visual, then zoom into scattered functions touching same data.

scenes.voice: When a system passes a few thousand lines, procedural code spreads state across globals and behavior across unrelated functions. Change what a payment is, and you touch validation, persistence, reporting, API formatting in different places.
scenes.visual: Diagram of global state with arrows to many functions, highlight duplication and cross-cutting changes.

scenes.voice: The constraint is real: evolving domain, multiple teams, need for testability, cost of change. You need a way to localize state and behavior so changes are bounded.
scenes.visual: Three icons: evolving domain, teams, testability, with cost of change rising.

scenes.voice: Reasonable first approach is to group related data and functions. That is the idea: an object is a small bounded context with a public contract and private invariants. Think bank account. You call deposit, withdraw, getBalance. You do not manipulate the ledger directly.
scenes.visual: Bank account box with private balance, public methods deposit/withdraw/getBalance. External caller only sees contract.

scenes.voice: This works because of four levers. Encapsulation hides implementation behind an interface so you can refactor internals without breaking callers. Abstraction exposes only the relevant concept. Polymorphism lets you call process on any payment provider and get correct behavior. Composition over inheritance lets you assemble small objects for flexible reuse.
Here is how it looks architecturally. The service depends on a contract, not concrete types.
scenes.visual: Mermaid flowchart showing Client to PaymentService to PaymentProcessor to StripeAdapter, PayPalAdapter, InvoiceAdapter via polymorphism.
scenes.mermaid:
flowchart LR
Client --> PaymentService
PaymentService --> PaymentProcessor
PaymentProcessor -->|polymorphism| StripeAdapter
PaymentProcessor -->|polymorphism| PayPalAdapter
PaymentProcessor -->|polymorphism| InvoiceAdapter

scenes.voice: Trade-off: OOP makes change cheaper inside a boundary but more expensive across boundaries if contracts are violated. Inheritance abuse creates fragile base classes. Anemic models leak invariants. Over-engineering adds complexity tax.
scenes.visual: Scale balancing cheap internal change vs expensive cross-boundary change, with warning icons for inheritance abuse and anemic model.

scenes.voice: Mental model: ask where are the invariants, what is the contract, and what happens to change cost when this object grows. Use OOP when domain entities have lifecycles and protected invariants. Avoid it for pure data transformation.
scenes.visual: Checklist appearing: invariants? contract? change cost? with domain entity examples Order, Account, Reservation.

mental_model: Treat an object as a small bounded context that owns state, enforces invariants, and exposes a contract. Decide by asking: where will state live, who enforces rules, and how painful is the next change.
final_takeaway: OOP exists to localize state and behavior so change is bounded and understandable.
